I would remind him that Bouri-not, in his fourth edition, in discussing these abstract resolutions, after having pointed out that it is impossible for members to move motions that involve directly the expenditure of money, says that they are intended to point out to the government the importance
The Budget-Mr. Knowles and necessity of such expenditures. An expenditure or a reduction in taxation amount to the same thing. The point I am making is that when members of this house vote on a motion asking the government to consider something they are, in fact, expressing their opinion on the substance of the question which the government is asked to consider.
The parliamentary assistant tried today to make a great deal out of the fact it was only a request to consider. He parroted the words of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) yesterday, when the minister interjected a remark in the speech of the member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). As recorded at page 1486 of Hansard for April 22, 1952, the Minister of Finance said:
The Minister of Finance never refuses to consider any suggestions, whether it is from the House of Commons or from any other place. That was the reason the resolution was not voted down.
Most of us did not come to this house yesterday. We have been here for some time and we know what the practice is with respect to private members' resolutions. If the government does not like them and is not prepared to consider what their substance calls for, they are either talked out or voted down. In some cases, they are withdrawn at the request of the government, when the sponsor is a government member.
Let me remind the parliamentary assistant and the minister what happened a year ago. On February 26, 1951, I moved a motion asking the government to consider the advisability of introducing legislation to amend the Income Tax Act so as to provide for the deductibility of trade union dues. The opening words of that motion were identical, to every jot and tittle, to the motion that I introduced this year on March 26 with respect to the deductibility of medical expenses. I made sure that the wording was identical. My motion of a year ago asked for consideration. Did the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) say on that occasion, as he said to my leader yesterday, that the Minister of Finance never refuses to consider any suggestion whether from the House of Commons or any other place, and that is the reason the resolution was not voted down? Not on your life; the resolution was voted down on February 26, 1951, by the majority on the government side. I was very pleased that in that particular case the Minister of Finance changed his mind some time between February 26, 1951, and the date of his budget. When he brought down his budget of April 10, 1951, he did carry out, in part at least, the request in that resolution, even though the resolution itself had been defeated.
Let me remind the parliamentary assistant and the house generally of some other private
1538	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Knowles members' resolutions. I had one that was defeated on October 3, 1949. It asked the government simply to consider the appointment of a royal commission to look into the loss of pension rights by Canadian Pacific Railway workers who were involved in the 1919 strike. Did the government say they were prepared to consider anything, and therefore would not vote that down? No, they were against the substance of what was involved in that resolution, and so it was voted down by the government majority.
On February 19, 1951, the member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) introduced a resolution which merely asked that the government consider the advisability of establishing a committee to consider certain aspects of cigarette smoking. It was only a request for consideration. Did the government say, as the Minister of Finance said yesterday, that the government is prepared to consider anything? No, they said, through the mouth of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), that no doubt the member for Fort William would be satisfied that his case had been made. He was asked to withdraw his motion. When some of us refused to give unanimous consent to the withdrawal of that motion, it was put to a vote. Was it allowed to pass because it was simply a request for consideration? Not on your life, it was defeated by the government majority.
The hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) has on a number of occasions introduced a private member's resolution with regard to soldier settlers. I am thinking particularly of the one on February 21, 1951, which asked for all that a private member can ask, that consideration be given to the granting of clear titles to certain soldier settlers. Did the government say, in the words of the Minister of Finance or of the parliamentary assistant, that the government will consider anything and therefore allow it to pass? No, it was defeated by a recorded vote with the government majority seeing to it that it was defeated.
On February 22, 1951, the member for Chambly-Rouville (Mr. Pinard) introduced a motion asking that the government consider, just consider, the abolition of tolls on certain bridges in the Montreal area. When the debate was just about over the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) indicated that a very good case had been made, that it would be studied, and perhaps in view of that undertaking the member for Chambly-Rouville would be prepared to withdraw his motion. Why did not the Minister of Transport do what the Minister of Finance said yesterday and say that the government was prepared to consider anything, so the motion could pass? No, they did not want to commit 

themselves to the substance of the motion so the member for Chambly-Rouville was asked to withdraw it. He was prepared to do so, but when some of us said we were not prepared to give unanimous consent to the withdrawal of the motion it was put to a vote and it was defeated, despite the fact the Minister of Transport had just spoken sympathetically about it.
I could go on referring to motions put by other hon. members, such as the one by the member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) asking for the decentralization of industry. This motion has not come to a vote as yet; it has been talked out and that is- another means that is employed from time to time to defeat these motions. What is crystal clear to anyone who wants to face the facts is that when a motion has in it something which the government does not want to have itself committed to, it sees to it that that motion does not pass, even though it technically asks simply for consideration. It either sees to it that it is defeated by the government majority in this house or if it is a Liberal motion it sometimes persuades its sponsor to withdraw the motion. Or again, the motion may be talked out. Therefore, I contend that though my motion asked for the only thing a private member can request, consideration, nevertheless the fact that it passed unanimously means that this house expressed its view not only that consideration should be given to my proposal but expressed its thought on the substance of that motion.
Hon. members who were in the house on the afternoon of Wednesday, March 26, will remember the general feeling that was around the house. They will remember also the general feeling of satisfaction that the government had seen fit to accept the motion, and the hope that that would result in the principle being implemented when the budget was brought down. A short while ago the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sinclair) read his interjection in what I had to say on March 26, as recorded at page 828 of Hansard. May I read some of the rest of what I had to say on that same page, making it crystal clear that I fully recognized the technicality of the position but also that the house accepted the spirit of what I was advocating on that occasion. I said:
I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that I realize full well that the passing of this resolution does not mean the immediate legislative enactment of what it asks for. The resolution asks for all that a private member, under the rules of the house, can ask for, namely that the government give consideration to the proposal that the four per cent floor, in connection with medical expenses in relation to income tax, should be wiped out.

I take it that if this resolution is passed, since it has won the support of the government, the government will do what the resolution asks, namely will give consideration to that proposal. Naturally I hope the fact that this resolution is passed unanimously by this house will suggest to the government that that consideration should be favourable.
The parliamentary assistant, who says today that he was watching me like a hawk, did not interrupt at that point. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that at that time I stated the position with exactitude. The position was that technically it was a request for consideration; but in spirit, in terms of what was the thinking and the opinion of the members of this house, we were expressing our unanimous view on a specific idea and we were hopeful that the government would go along with that idea when it brought down the budget on April 8.
People outside the house are not impressed with the technical aspect of this matter even to the extent that I have been prepared to spell it out. People outside the house see this whole picture in terms of parliament, which consists of 262 members, which they believe to be superior to the cabinet of 20 members. People outside this house-and most of us have been home during the Easter recess and have obtained the views of the man in the street-simply understand that the 262 of us, the entire house, expressed a view but then one member in the cabinet rejected that view. The man in the street simply cannot understand such defiance of parliament.
In the press of the country many references have been made to this affair. That is natural, because the morning after the motion passed on March 26 in support of the abolition of the four per cent floor, it was headline news in most of the papers in the country; and within the next few days a great many papers editorialized on it favourably. They were pleased to see that the government had accepted a private member's motion and in particular a motion from the opposition side of the house. Editorial writers in general approved of the substance of that motion and anticipated that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), after giving it his consideration, would certainly carry out the wish of the house.
It is therefore only natural that many of these newspapers are annoyed over what happened and are now beginning to express their views. For example, I have here an editorial that appeared in the Winnipeg Tribune of Thursday, April 17. The heading of that editorial is significant; it is "Parliament be Blowed". The editorial reads in part as follows:
Just how much Influence parliament has with the government in some things was clearly shown by what happened to deductions from income tax for medical expenses in the current budget.
The Budget-Mr. Knowles
On March 26 Stanley Knowles. M.P. for Winnipeg, introduced a resolution urging the government to consider the introduction of legislation to permit taxpayers to deduct from their incomes, before computing the amount of income taxes to be paid, the entire amount of medical expenses rather than merely the portion in excess of four per cent of their taxable income, as the act now stands.
The editorial goes on to point out that this motion received the support of members in all sections of the house. It points out also that there was some discussion on other aspects of the problem, notably references to the ceiling, but says that in the end no change was made in my motion and that it passed in its original form asking for the one change, namely the removal of the four per cent floor. Then towards the end of the editorial the Tribune says:
Mr. Abbott chose to ignore what amounted to a directive from the Commons and followed something that had been merely mentioned in the debate. He raised the ceilings-something that would benefit only taxpayers with phenomenal ill health.
This is another instance of the parliament-be-damned attitude of the present administration.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the parliamentary assistant and those on the other side can argue, if they wish, that it is not technically correct for the Winnipeg Tribune to say that that motion was a directive. But that is the view of people who look objectively at the functioning of parliament. They see these 262 members pass a motion unanimously. To them-and in practical terms they are correct-it amounted to a directive from the Commons and the Minister of Finance chose to ignore that directive.
I have here another editorial. This time it is from the Globe and Mail of Toronto and it appears in the issue of Friday, April 11. The heading is "A Loaf and a Stone". I will read only two or three sentences of it:
A minor item in Finance Minister Abbott's budget precisely illustrates the contempt with which the federal cabinet treats the views of parliament and the needs of the public. In this instance, it seems to have made a special effort to express that contempt, to assert its lordly disregard of the taxpayers and their elected representatives.
Then the writer goes on to point out that a change has been proposed in the budget to raise the ceiling to $1,000 and to $2,000. Then he says:
This is exactly the opposite of what parliament wants; and in fact, has asked for.
Then the editorial goes on to spell out the terms of the resolution in language similar, as a matter of fact, to that in the editorial that I have just read. Then I quote this:
The cabinet was not satisfied merely to deny that request, but cynically twisted it right around, giving parliament what it did not seek, and refusing it what it did ... It accepted the principle endorsed by parliament, but handed it back in such a way as to make parliament look absurd. Asked for a loaf, it grinningly gave a stone.
1540	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Knowles
If parliament must accept the insult, it is the taxpayers who must accept the injury; particularly those in the middle income brackets.
I have here as well a letter to the editor that appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press. I really would not expect the Winnipeg Free Press to take my part against the Liberal government, but at least they went this far. They ran this letter a few days ago. It appeared on Saturday, April 19, 1952, and it is over the signature of J. W. Gilbert of Hanover, Ontario. This is an exceedingly interesting letter because it deals not only with the amazing situation that the cabinet could ignore the unanimous vote of the members of the House of Commons but also deals with an important point of substance in relation to the question itself, namely that of abolishing the four per cent floor.
I will come back to that matter in just a moment. Before I do so, I want to sum up this part of my remarks by saying that I regard what the government did in this respect as one of the worst exhibitions that I lave seen in this parliament for a long time. This government is asking the people of this rountry to spend billions of dollars for the lefence of democracy, yet the government is scuttling democracy right here in the House )f Commons. The whole approach of this Government to parliamentary democracy is such as to spread cynicism in the minds of )ur people and to weaken the support of our leople for what is so often called our way >f life. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that times ike the present call for greater adherence han ever to the principles of democracy; md when a group of 262 members of parlia-nent unanimously express their view as to vhat should be done, it should be carried out >y the government of the day.
I now want to go on and say a bit more ibout the substance of the matter itself >ecause I dare to hope that the government nay reconsider its position on this matter wen at this session, even before this budget s put through. I would say that one of the vays to bring that event about is for a good leal to be said about this matter, not only >y those of us on the opposition side of the louse who perhaps feel most annoyed by chat has happened but also by members on he government side of the house, many of idiom probably feel the same way. We all iave the experience in parliament of know-ng that copies of letters written to us are ometimes sent to members in other parties, t happens both ways. There have come to ly desk copies of letters that have been sent a members on the Liberal side of the house, sking their views on what happened, and rging them to call upon the Minister of 'inance (Mr. Abbott) during the course of


this budget debate to change his position with respect to this four per cent floor, and I hope that that will be done and that the government will yet give favourable consideration to the request of this house, which was expressed in that vote on March 26.
Now, with respect to the question itself, the parliamentary assistant has not yet dealt with the point that we made in the previous debate as to the unfairness of allowing the deduction for charitable expenses right from the first dollar up to ten per cent of income; whereas in the case of medical expenses the first dollar is not allowed; in fact, nothing is allowed until you reach this four per cent floor. I need not go into that again at length; I have done it on two or three occasions when I have spoken on the matter. But may 1 say that many of the letters I get on this subject deal with it, and people generally simply do not understand that unfairness. We urge that if people are allowed to make deductions for charitable donations, which they make voluntarily, without any floor, the same attitude should be taken toward medical expenses, which are made involuntarily and of necessity.
The Minister of Finance and the parliamentary assistant have a great deal to say about four per cent being the average medical expense. Well, that same concept might be applied to charitable donations, but it is not. As for this whole concept of averages, Mr. Speaker, surely anyone like the Minister of Finance or the parliamentary assistant who deals in mathematical matters must know how deceiving averages can be. I believe the average personal income in this country at the present time is something over $1,000 per year per person, including every man, woman and child. That would work out to an average personal income per family of about $5,000 per year. But it is no help to the family on $2,000 a year to know that the average is $5,000 a year. As for average medical expenses, the fact of the matter is that what hits the person is not an abstract average but the fact that if he has medical expenses at all, he is probably paying more than the average because somebody else is fortunate enough to go through a year without medical expenses. Statisticians tell us, for example, that about one out of every seven persons is hospitalized every year. Well, to those who are the ones in the seven and who need assistance it is no help simply to be told that four per cent of their income spent on medical costs is an average and therefore cannot be allowed.
This whole business of averages being deceiving was brought out again today in what the parliamentary assistant tried to do, which I thought was not a very sound analysis. He suggested that if we removed

this four per cent floor it would reduce the taxable income by four per cent, and would reduce the income tax accruing to the federal treasury by four per cent of the amount estimated by the Minister of Finance. I take it that is where he got his $48 million, which is roughly four per cent of the $1,200 million odd which it is expected will accrue from the personal income tax in the current fiscal year. But I would point out to him that when you abolish the four per cent floor it does not mean that every taxpayer in the country reduces the amount of the income on which he then pays by four per cent, because a great. many people will have no medical expenses at all during the course of the year. Then, after you have accounted for that mistake in the parliamentary assistant's reasoning you have to look at another fact. People pay different rates of taxes on their income, depending upon what bracket they are in. Some will be in higher brackets; some in lower. I submit that he has done something that amounts to oversimplification in just assuming that the loss would be $48 million. But whatever it is, Mr. Speaker, his point of course was not concern for the amount, as to whether it was small or large. He sought to make the point that the $48 million would apparently come off everybody on the average, and everybody on the average would in turn have to make it up. My point is that it would not be a saving spread evenly; it would be spread according to the individual taxpayer's medical expenses. I submit that, like all the rest of his argument about averages, what he said was no argument at all.
I said a few moments ago that this letter to the Winnipeg Free Press from Mr. J. W. Gilbert touched on a very important point. He points out that people who have to use certain drugs right along like insulin, for example, in many cases get no benefit at all of the deduction for medical expenses. A year ago, when the Minister of Finance added insulin, cortisone and ACTH and one other drug to the list of items that could be classified as medical expenses, a great ado was made of it by the government. But a great many people who have to use these drugs find that thait provision is no help to them, because their expenditures on these drugs in the course of a year, while they may be heavy, while they may be a blow to them, and while it is a blow that they have to meet year in and year out, will not in any one year add up to more than four per cent of the taxpayer's net income. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, my point is that these people are not comforted at all by being told that four per cent of their income for medical expenses is an average. Indeed you are giving no benefit to people who are faced with recurring
The Budget-Mr. Knowles medical expenses and recurring costs for drugs of this nature. You can only do it if you are prepared to wipe out that four per cent floor.
The parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance quoted again today the remarks that he had quoted from the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll), and which he gave to the house on March 26. I was very glad when he made that quotation in the first place, and I was glad that he repeated it today, because it indeed is the whole point of our asking for the removal of the four per cent floor, and our suggesting that that is more important than raising the ceiling or making some of the other changes that might be suggested.
Let me read again what the parliamentary assistant said as reported at page 820 of Hansard for March 26:
The hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) raised this proposal of removing or lowering the four per cent item, and pointed out that this would give the maximum help to the little man, the man with just enough income to place him in the income tax bracket.
I concur wholly in the sentiment expressed by the hon. member for Spadina, and I must say that it was about at that point in the speech of the parliamentary assistant on March 26, when he quoted the hon. member for Spadina, that it dawned on me that my motion had a chance of passing. Here was an admission by the parliamentary assistant, despite the difficulties that he had listed, and other difficulties he might add yet, here was an admission that what I was asking for would be of assistance to the little fellow, So I began to realize there was a possibility of my motion passing, and sure enough, a couple of pages later, he indicated that the Minister of Finance was prepared to give consideration to that proposal.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, I need not take the time to repeat the arguments with respect tc substance that are in the speech I made on March 26, and that are in the speeches tha1 I have made in former years on this subject. But I do make this passing reference tc them, because I think it is our job now in this House of Commons not only to condemn the government as strongly as we can foi having hoodwinked the people of Canada on this matter, but it is our job to try to persuade the government to repair this damage at this session. I emphasize the words "a1 this session", because there is no doubt in my mind that if it is not done at this session il will be done next year, or in whatever budgel that comes on the eve of an election.
This will not cost the federal treasury a great deal of money; but it is an issue oi concern to the little man, as the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) has said. It is oi

The Budget-Mr. Knowles concern to the people right across this country; and there is no doubt in my mind that this four per cent floor will go before the government goes to the country in another election.
I suggest that that is not a proper discharge of responsibility. That is not loyalty to the principles and practices of democracy-just to fool around with budgetary and taxation matters in that way, leaving desirable changes until election time. If the principle I have set out is good-and it is good, because the whole house said so on March 26, and the newspapers from coast to coast are saying so, as well as the little people of Canada from coast to coast-then let us have it at this session of parliament.
Another reason for my continuing to make this plea for action at the present session, despite the fact that the budget has come down and that it is only very seldom that changes are made after its presentation to the house, is that there have been exceptional occasions when changes have been made. Dne of those exceptional occasions was one to which I made reference on March 26, oecause it related to this very question. At the risk of repeating what I said then, I would state briefly that in 1944, when Mr. [lsley brought down his budget, he included .n his budget resolutions two resolutions relating to the deductibility of medical jxpenses for income tax purposes. They were resolutions numbers 4 and 5 in the list le tabled on June 26, 1944. I shall not take ;ime to read them, but I will point out that neither of those resolutions included any reference to lowering the floor or raising the reiling. Despite that fact, when we reached committee of ways and means to consider ;he budget resolution, and got down to -esolutions numbers 4 and 5, the committee witnessed a lengthy debate in which the ninister of finance was asked to raise the ceiling and to lower the floor.
Hon. members from all sides of the house md in all parties participated in that debate, indeed, I pointed out on March 26 that even ;he Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) participated in it. I said at that ;ime that in those days he was somewhat closer to the taxpayers' point of view than re is today. He wanted funeral expenses to )e included as medical expenses for purposes cf the act.
The then minister of finance took part in ;he debate and accepted the reasonableness )f some of the arguments. In the main, lowever, he stood up against them, and most >f us in the house at that time thought that t would be the same old story, that we were

making a case for something we would get, but that we would get it one or two sessions later. To our pleasant surprise, however, following the debate which took place in midsummer-July, I believe it was-a bill was brought in to amend the Income War Tax Act, in conformity with what had been contained in the budget resolutions. We found, however, that the bill included something that had not been in those resolutions, namely a section to raise the ceiling and a section to lower the floor.
Prior to that time the floor had stood at 5 per cent, and we had pleaded that it be reduced to 2 per cent or 3 per cent. Mr. Ilsley met us part way-I admit it was only a little way, but at least it was part way-by reducing the floor to 4 per cent. This was welcomed as a demonstration of the fact that once in a while the government does pay attention to a debate in the house. My hope is that there will be sufficient debate at this session with respect to medical expenses so that, when the bill to amend the Income Tax Act is brought in, the government will go a step farther than is provided for in the resolutions, and will make the change asked for on March 26, by way of abolishing this floor altogether.
I do not know what the cost to the treasury would be, but I am satisfied the parliamentary assistant is not correct in suggesting that it would be $48 million. I am satisfied he is not following a correct method of computation, when he arrives at that figure. But. whether it is greater or less than that amount, it is a principle of justice and of fairness we are asking for. And in this case it is even more than that. We are asking for a recognition by the government of the clearly expressed wish of parliament, instead of sheer defiance.
Let us not have any more of the attempts we had yesterday, when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) interrupted my leader, or the attempt today by the parliamentary assistant, when they tried to hide behind a technicality. Certainly the motion asked that the government consider the matter, as do all private members' motions. The government knows that is as far as private members' motions can go; but it also knows that it looks at each and every one of these motions-and not just at the words down to the word "consideration." It looks at the substance following that word. If the substance is one to which the government does not wish to commit itself, the motion does not pass. But in this instance the government allowed the motion to pass, and to pass

unanimously. We had every right to believe that that meant approval of the proposal contained in that resolution.
I submit the criticism we level at the government for ignoring that clearly expressed wish is one which reflects the thinking of the people of this country. I call upon the government to pay attention to that thinking, to make the change at this session and to abolish the four per cent floor under medical expenses in relation to income tax.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is well known that I am not a financial critic, but I appreciate the ability of those who are able to do that which I cannot do. I congratulate the financial critic of the official opposition on pulling the budget to pieces, and leaving it as a whole. I think he did a good job.
Today the parliamentary assistant did what I was going to do, when he read from the Financial Post. By doing so he has saved me from that necessity. I read the Financial Post because I can learn something from it, and because usually it tells the truth. I would add to that, that outside the House of Commons the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) is held as an outstanding financial expert.
I know we do not like to pay taxes; nobody does. I would rather spend a dollar on cigarettes than on taxes. But taxes have to be paid; and I am one who did not expect the budget this year to contain many reductions in taxation. I did expect there would be reductions in some respects, especially on articles connected with household needs. And those taxes have been reduced.
The people of Fort William know that I have worked for the last number of years to have old age pensions brought to the point where they would be helpful to people over seventy years, and to those in need. Because old age pensions and old age security measures were passed, almost unanimously, I cannot for the life of me see how the amount of taxes could fail to be higher. We congratulate the Minister of Finance upon his taxation measures, and his ability to reduce the national debt. Taxes have been increased since we came into this house. Not long ago I was criticized in Fort William because of the amount of taxes being collected by the dominion government and the surpluses that had been built up. I asked this man what taxes he paid in 1935, 1936 or 1940 and he wanted to send me to the hot place. I said that I was not going there, neither was I going to take our taxes there.
We should realize that taxes are insurance against war, unemployment, poverty, old age, crime and the growth of unpleasant ideologies.
The Budget-Mr. Mclvor If this insurance is being increased to include other ways of helping Canadians then our taxes must go up.
I want to tell the Minister of Finance one place where he can get more money. The Shebandowan district contains large quantities of nickel, gold, iron ore, chromium, tungsten and other minerals. The International Nickel Company should be encouraged to open up the claims they have in that district instead of allowing them to remain idle. I expect to see the minister of mines and ask him his advice.
There are two ways in which the minister could spend a little more. I am not going to ask the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) to build a gymnasium for the House of Commons, but it is needed. Members who are interested in keeping their health have found other ways of doing that. I was thrilled today to receive from the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees) a challenge from members of the opposition and the press gallery to members on this side of the house to meet on the first Thursday in June for our ball game. I accepted willingly.
There is another important way in which the minister could spend some money, to take care of our incapacitated. I am going to lay this matter on the doorstep of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) because I remember how he blotted out little nests of Irish, Scotch, English, Ukrainians, Italians, Russians, Germans and others and made us one Canadian nation. That was a fine thing to do. I remember also how he brought in the scheme to aid hospitals with construction and hospitalization costs. Then last year he brought in his old age assistance and old age security measures.
I am going to lay on his doorstep a problem that is just as important, the taking care of those who are incapacitated. I have a number of letters here but I shall not read them all. I have a long list of incapacitated which I received from the trades and labour council of Fort William, but I shall not read it. However, I should like to read one letter from outside Fort William, from Cape Breton. This is a mother writing, and she said:
I have a girl 35 years a victim ol polio, and a boy 32 years. They are both helpless cripples. They have never had a cent they could call their own. Their father was hurt six years ago in the mine and will never be able to work again. You can imagine the hardships they endure.

I shall be very glad to do it. The writer is Mrs. Neil K. McNeil.
I think the incapacitated can be divided into three classes. First are those who can get around in wheel chairs, on crutches or in some other way in order to earn a living. Then there are those who cannot get around but who have the use of their hands, their mind, their eyes, their speech and are able to earn a little. Then there are those who cannot get around at all and who cannot earn one cent.
Up to a day or two ago I thought that these were the forgotten people. We have old age pensions, mothers' allowances, family allowances, workmen's compensation and unemployment insurance, but these measures do not touch these people at all. Many of these people have relatives who are mighty proud and do not want to send them to homes for incurables. They want to keep them in their own homes just as John Bunyan held in his heart his little blind girl and kept her with him. These people do everything in order to keep their own folks in their own homes.
While I do not want an extra session this year I think the government would, be well advised to take up this matter at this session and see that something is done this year, or at least at the beginning of next year. This is one of the outstanding needs of Canada. To think that we have such people in a Christian country whose program is to feed the hungry, clothe the naked and visit the sick! These people cannot earn a cent. I can take you into a home where a pretty little girl, who is completely helpless, just sits in the corner. She must be fed, she must be dressed, she must be carried everywhere. Yet there is not a dollar for her. Surely the Minister of National Health and Welfare has enough heart to feel that these things should not be.
As I said, I thought that these people were not recognized, that no attention was being paid to them, but the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) has indicated that something is being done. He informs me that officials of the appropriate provincial departments, officials of welfare agencies and officials of the Department of National Health and Welfare, the Department of Veterans Affairs and the Department of Labour are co-operating under a national council to promote as a joint effort the medical and vocational rehabilitation of the disabled.
The first meeting of this council was held in Ottawa in February last. The object of the council is to co-ordinate all existing facilities for helping the disabled to overcome their handicaps and to equip themselves for work and wage earning as was so successfully accomplished with Canada's veterans. At the February meeting Dr. McNally, chancellor of the University of Alberta, was elected chairman and Father Beaudin of Montreal, vice-chairman, with a very strong executive. This indicates that the three dominion departments are combining with the provincial governments to provide for the incapacitated. I like to refer to the suggestions of people on the other side when they suggest something good. Premier Frost of Ontario is going all-out to help the incapacitated of that province, and I am sure that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg), and the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe) will co-operate. I appreciate very much what has been done for the Fort William district by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). Many things have been done which have helped us. Now this further need is faced not only in Fort William but all over Canada. We think it is an outstanding need, and I will not support an increase in any other pension until this matter is thoroughly considered and settled.
On motion of Mrs. Fairclough the debate was adjourned.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Tomorrow we will continue the debate on the budget. Members may want to know when the house will replace the time taken from private members for the setting up of the committee on redistribution. Tomorrow we expect to put in Votes and Proceedings a notice of motion which will take away next Monday as a private members' day but with the understanding that on that day we will give private members the same time as was taken for government business last Monday.

So that there will be no misunderstanding with respect to the motion of the Minister of Transport to set up the committee having to do with Canadian National Railways, will that be the first order of business tomorrow or the budget?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I think we should take the motion of the Minister of Transport first because from the way he explained it today I think it is urgent. Therefore that will be the first item tomorrow.
At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
